drills.q: What's the fundamental tradeoff between server-side sessions and stateless JWTs?
drills.a: Sessions store an opaque ID looked up server-side on every request, so revocation is an instant row deletion; JWTs encode state in a signed artifact verified locally with no lookup, removing a network round trip but leaving nothing to delete -- a valid JWT stays valid until it expires regardless of server-side wishes.

drills.q: Are JWTs 'just worse' than sessions since they can't be revoked instantly?
drills.a: No -- JWTs trade instant revocability for zero-lookup verification. Production systems needing both use a hybrid: short-lived JWT access tokens plus a server-tracked, revocable refresh token.

drills.q: Walk through killing a compromised user's access under pure-JWT vs the hybrid model.
drills.a: Pure JWT: no action invalidates an issued token; it stays valid until its own exp regardless of password resets elsewhere. Hybrid: revoke the refresh token (DB flag/delete) immediately; the current access token still works until its own short TTL elapses, so worst-case exposure equals the access-token TTL, typically minutes not days.

drills.q: If an attacker already holds a valid unexpired access token when you revoke the refresh token, are they locked out immediately?
drills.a: No -- that access token keeps working until it naturally expires; revoking the refresh token only stops new access tokens from being minted. This is why access-token TTL should be chosen based on tolerance for this residual-risk window, not set long for convenience.

drills.q: Why did the industry move toward tokens if Redis-backed sessions can scale fine?
drills.a: The real win is removing the network dependency for cross-service and cross-domain verification -- any of N services verifies a JWT locally with zero central-store calls, which matters for microservice fan-out and multi-backend mobile/SPA clients. Redis sessions scale fine for raw QPS to one service; the pain is specifically at cross-service fan-out.

drills.q: A junior engineer wants to store the full permission list in the JWT payload to avoid DB hits. What's wrong?
drills.a: A revoked permission won't take effect until the token expires (authz staleness bug), and large claim sets bloat every request. Keep JWTs to sub/exp and a few coarse, slow-changing claims; look up fine-grained or fast-changing permissions server-side by ID.

drills.q: Why does putting a JWT in a cookie vs an Authorization header change the security model, not just transport?
drills.a: A cookie auto-attaches on matching-origin requests, reintroducing CSRF exposure (mitigate with SameSite + anti-CSRF token); a header-based Bearer token needs explicit JS to attach it, avoiding CSRF but requiring JS-accessible storage, which exposes it to XSS exfiltration if kept in localStorage. Neither is unconditionally safer.

drills.q: What's the actual latency difference between a session lookup and JWT verification, and when does it matter?
drills.a: Redis session lookup ~0.5-2ms with a network hop; local JWT verification sub-0.5ms with zero hops. Immaterial for most systems next to overall request latency; matters at extreme fan-out (hundreds of internal calls per user request) or very high QPS where the session store becomes a capacity concern.

drills.q: Design the token strategy for a banking mobile app where a stolen phone must be lockable within seconds.
drills.a: Very short access-token TTL (60-300s) paired with a server-tracked, device-bound refresh token. 'Lock this device' revokes the refresh token, taking full effect within the access token's short TTL -- a few minutes worst case on an already-open session, zero on any new request.

drills.q: Someone claims 'sessions are legacy, tokens are the modern approach.' Push back.
drills.a: Both remain in active correct use: a server-rendered monolith on one backend cluster gains real instant revocation from sessions at negligible cost. Systems needing cross-service fan-out or cross-domain SSO benefit from tokens, but the honest modern default is the hybrid -- neither pure sessions nor pure stateless tokens -- reintroducing a small amount of server-side state exactly where revocation matters most.

drills.q: An incident runbook says 'for a compromised account, disable the user in the admin panel.' Why is that incomplete under pure-JWT auth?
drills.a: Disabling the user changes a DB flag a future login check would see, but does nothing to an already-issued JWT, which carries no reference to that flag and is verified purely by signature and expiry -- the attacker's existing token keeps working until natural expiry. The runbook needs an explicit refresh-token revocation or deny-list step.

drills.q: When would you recommend OAuth token introspection (RFC 7662) over the local-JWT-plus-refresh hybrid?
drills.a: When resource servers don't hold or trust the verification key material directly, or when centralized real-time visibility into every token check is needed for compliance -- introspection trades some latency (a cacheable network call per verification) for centralized control local JWT verification structurally can't provide.
